Sign for software company Netapp at the company's office in the Silicon Valley, San Jose, California, December 18, 2021. Photo courtesy Tech Trends. (Photo by Gado/Getty Images)
Several announcements at INSIGHT highlighted the AI opportunity BofA noted.
NetApp and Supermicro announced jointly validated infrastructure targeting AI factories, neoclouds, enterprise deployments and sovereign AI.
A new NetApp storage service will run natively on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with general availability planned within the next 12 months.

NetApp Inc. (NTAP) is giving investors another reason to focus on its AI strategy. Bank of America raised its price target on NTAP stock to $220 from $200 after attending the company's INSIGHT 2026 event, saying artificial intelligence is expanding the addressable market for the storage provider.
According to the Fly, BofA analyst Wamsi Mohan maintained a Neutral rating, but said the firm is applying a higher valuation multiple to the incremental opportunity created by AI. The shift comes as NetApp expands its AI infrastructure strategy through new partnerships with Supermicro Corp (SMCI) and Oracle (ORCL).

Several announcements at INSIGHT illustrated the AI opportunity highlighted by BofA.

NetApp and Super Micro Computer Inc. (SMCI) announced a strategic collaboration to create jointly validated AI infrastructure spanning large-scale AI factories, enterprise deployments, neoclouds and sovereign AI projects.
The companies are pairing Supermicro’s compute and rack-scale systems with NetApp’s data platform to improve graphics processing unit (GPU) utilization and reduce the complexity of deploying AI infrastructure.
Novus Takes Aim At Large-Scale AI Infrastructure
NetApp also introduced Novus, a new architecture aimed at AI infrastructure providers operating large GPU environments. The company said it is being built to support a zettabyte-scale file system and keep large GPU clusters supplied with data.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Oracle Partnership Expands NetApp's Cloud Reach
NetApp’s push extends beyond dedicated AI infrastructure.
The company and Oracle Corp. (ORCL) announced Oracle Cloud Infrastructure NetApp Storage Service, which will bring NetApp ONTAP data-management capabilities natively into Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
The fully managed service is intended to support migration and management of AI and enterprise workloads, including databases, virtualized environments and AI data pipelines. General availability is planned within the next 12 months.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
NetApp also used INSIGHT to announce new AI Data Engine capabilities designed to discover, govern, and make enterprise data available for AI where it already resides, rather than requiring companies to create additional copies of that data.

By Trader EdgeSeptember 30, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Oracle shares climbed approximately 4% on Tuesday, ending a four-session decline.
The rally followed the introduction of Fusion Claw, an AI governance platform for agentic applications.
Two additional compliance solutions, Nexus Case Flow and Nexus Reach, were announced for financial services firms.
Oracle and NetApp revealed a managed storage partnership, boosting NetApp shares by roughly 1%.
Despite Tuesday’s gains, Oracle stock remains down 29% for the year and 56% off its 52-week peak.
Oracle stock advanced roughly 4% during Tuesday’s session, finishing near $138 and halting a four-day slide. The upward movement followed the company’s announcement of multiple AI-focused products designed for its cloud infrastructure platform.
The centerpiece of these announcements was Fusion Claw, a governed execution runtime designed specifically for Oracle’s Fusion Agentic Applications suite.
Fusion Claw validates and approves autonomous AI agent actions as they occur. According to Oracle, this framework enables organizations to delegate more sophisticated tasks to AI systems while maintaining appropriate oversight mechanisms.
The platform immediately supports 25 specialist-grade applications, forming part of a broader collection of 75 agentic applications currently operating on Oracle’s cloud platform.
CEO Mike Sicilia characterized the technology as a workforce enabler. He explained that allowing AI to manage more operational tasks enables personnel to concentrate on strategic growth initiatives and customer relationships.
Financial Services Compliance Solutions Introduced
Beyond Fusion Claw, Oracle Financial Services introduced two additional products: Nexus Case Flow and Nexus Reach.
These solutions target banking institutions and other financial organizations. They leverage agentic AI to streamline anti-financial crime investigations and regulatory compliance processes.
In a separate development, Oracle and NetApp unveiled a fully managed storage offering. The service integrates NetApp’s enterprise-grade storage capabilities directly into Oracle’s cloud infrastructure, facilitating AI workload management for enterprise clients.
NetApp shares rose approximately 1% to $206.32 following the announcement, extending the storage provider’s winning streak to five consecutive sessions.
Tuesday’s rally represents a brief respite in what has been a challenging year for Oracle shareholders. The stock has declined 29% year-to-date and trades 56% beneath its October 2025 peak of $313.
Volatility has characterized recent trading, with the stock experiencing 36 price swings exceeding 5% over the past twelve months. Market observers interpret Tuesday’s advance as a response to concrete product announcements rather than a fundamental reassessment of the company.
Just five days prior, Oracle shares fell 3.4% after reports emerged that the company had issued a “force majeure” notice related to its New Mexico data center development. The facility, designated as Project Jupiter, represents a critical component of the broader Stargate AI infrastructure initiative.
The notice was designed to shield Oracle from escalating expenses should the project fail to meet its 2028 completion target. The communication was directed to a Blue Owl Capital subsidiary, which also experienced stock price declines following the disclosure.
Project Jupiter has encountered regulatory challenges, community resistance, and environmental scrutiny. Financial reports also indicated that $18 billion in project-related debt is currently trading at distressed valuations.
Oracle countered concerns by affirming to CNBC its “full commitment to New Mexico.” Co-CEO Clay Magouyrk additionally assured analysts during the September 10 earnings presentation that the project would not impact fiscal 2027 revenue or profit projections.
The company delivered robust first-quarter performance earlier this month, with cloud infrastructure revenue surging 121% year-over-year to reach $7.4 billion.
The next significant event for investors is Oracle’s investor day scheduled for October 28, coinciding with the company’s Oracle AI World conference running from October 25 through October 28.

NetApp Bets On Peak:AIO Acquisition To Provide New Performance Firepower In AI Data Battle
NetApp’s planned Peak:AIO acquisition strengthens its AI infrastructure and high-performance computing push, adding parallel NFS technology that channel partners can use to address enterprise AI factories, massive data workloads and tougher performance demands.
Intelligent data infrastructure technology developer NetApp Friday unveiled the planned acquisition of Peak:AIO, a developer of next-generation metadata architecture and high-performance parallel file systems.
Arindam Banerjee, NetApp’s chief platform and technology officer, told CRN that NetApp is acquiring Peak:AIO as a way to provide the orchestration to build large-scale environments.
“Peak:AIO works with a number of large national laboratories,” he said. “It is a part of Lattice, which we are very interested in.”
[Related: The 50 Coolest Software-Defined Storage Vendors: The 2026 Storage 100]
Lattice, which was unveiled in June, was developed in a collaboration involving Peak:AIO and the Los Alamos National Laboratory. Peak:AIO called Lattice the industry’s first open-source pNFS, or parallel NFS, metadata server.
Peak:AIO said Lattice provides for a new distributed metadata architecture aimed at eliminating one of the most persistent constraints in large-scale AI and high-performance computing infrastructure to provide ultra-fast, parallel access to massive datasets continuously and reliably to meet the needs high-performance AI workloads including training, running inference at scale, and serving agentic AI applications.
Banerjee said the Peak:AIO technology will help NetApp better address enterprise and institution requirements for building AI factories. The Peak:AIO technology is already in use at several national laboratories and high-performance computing environments, he said.
Banerjee declined to disclose how much NetApp is paying for Peak:AIO or when the acquisition is expected to close. More details around the integration will be available at the close, he said.
Peak:AIO CEO Roger Cummings wrote in a LinkedIn post that the fit between NetApp and Peak:AIO is a compelling one for customers.
“NetApp brings decades of enterprise experience, a global customer base, and a reputation built on helping some of the world’s largest organizations manage their most critical data,” Cummings wrote. “Peak:AIO brings a different piece of the equation: the performance, scale and efficiency required as AI and HPC fundamentally change what customers expect from their infrastructure. Together, we have an opportunity to help customers build the reliability and enterprise strength they expect from NetApp, with the performance AI and HPC workloads demand.”
The acquisition of Peak:AIO is a great move for NetApp, said Ned Engelke, chief technology officer at Evotek, a San Diego-based solution provider and NetApp channel partner.
Peak:AIO’s parallel NFS client is something NetApp has not had in its portfolio, Engelke told CRN.
“It allows you to have more throughput bandwidth, and probably lower latency, for file workloads, which would be beneficial there,” he said. “And that had been a point of competition against NetApp, generally, in the space. So I like that.”
Engelke said there are three elements of infrastructure: how to find and manage data, how to move that data around, and how to get it to whatever application needs it.
“So it’s fun for me to see NetApp doing this,” he said. “NetApp has the first two pieces. They have a good, robust control plane and data plane, and so it’s nice to see them making moves around improving how to get data into whatever application is being served.”
For example, Peak:AIO could help improve the performance of AI, Engelke said.
“We want to go fast,” he said. “We’re running on a GPU. We’re going to do all these different things. NetApp has done a lot over the last 10 years or so to work well with high-performance computing environments. Before this acquisition, they did co-development work with Nvidia to feed the cache, things like that. They’ve been doing really good stuff, but they’re making acquisitions and moves to expand the part of how they interact with a customer that takes data from their whole data control plane and then starts to make it more available to applications. That’s why I’m excited about it.”

NetApp Unveils AI Storage Architecture, Oracle Cloud Service And Agent Controls
NetApp announces its Novus AI storage architecture, Oracle Cloud Storage Service and updates to its AI data platform, security and sovereignty controls.
NetApp announced a storage architecture for AI data centers, a storage service with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and updates to its data platform Wednesday. The company framed the products around one problem: AI agents act on enterprise data at machine speed, while the infrastructure underneath was not built for that pace.
The centerpiece is NetApp Novus, an architecture that NetApp says is designed to exceed throughput of 100 terabytes per second and support hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Arindam Banerjee, NetApp's chief platform and technology officer, said storage stopped limiting applications years ago because those applications ran on CPUs. GPUs changed the equation, and new GPU generations arrive every 12 months.
Banerjee said market studies showed GPU utilization as low as 5% at some deployments. The company's press release puts the figure below 30% for storage designs that predate AI factories. Banerjee described the arithmetic behind the target: 50,000 GPUs, each drawing 2 gigabytes per second, add up to 100 terabytes per second from one namespace.
Novus separates metadata from the data path. Banerjee said the two run on separate nodes, so the lookups agents generate do not compete with large reads. Clients learn where data is placed and go to the right node for each task. The initial releases pair Novus Data Director, the metadata software, with ONTAP data services on AFF A90 systems, running on Supermicro infrastructure that NetApp has qualified. The system uses NFS and the pNFS flex files standard. Banerjee said competitors at this scale need a custom client to route traffic.
He gave figures to support the scaling claim. NetApp builds in blocks of 1 terabyte per second, added one at a time, in the manner of hyperscaler designs. A lab system at 10 terabytes per second runs today, he said, with linear scaling. Reaching 100 terabytes per second would take a federation of about 1,250 nodes. He said Google's managed Lustre announcement at Google Next reached 10 terabytes per second. He also said NetApp's internal tests reached 70,000 file creates per second.
Tony Palmer, chief analyst at Omdia, said the firm audited Novus and saw near-linear scaling as ONTAP clusters were added to the namespace. Omdia's modeling projects 100 TBps for sequential reads with dozens of exabytes of capacity. Novus is orderable today, and NetApp says software-defined deployments will follow.
NetApp and Oracle said they will launch Oracle Cloud Infrastructure NetApp Storage Service, a managed service that brings ONTAP data management to OCI. Customers will manage it through the OCI Console and SDKs, ONTAP APIs and existing operational workflows. General availability is planned within 12 months.
Jeff Baxter, NetApp's vice president of technical marketing, said the service will be an Oracle product built on ONTAP software. He noted that Azure NetApp Files, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Google Cloud NetApp Volumes already exist, which makes Oracle the fourth of the largest clouds to carry a first-party ONTAP offering.
"Enterprises shouldn't have to rebuild their data infrastructure to move to the cloud," said Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
Baxter opened the briefing with a Gartner projection that 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific AI agents this year and that agents will handle 15% of daily business decisions by 2028. He said cost per token becomes the constraint as adoption grows.
NetApp's answer on data is to leave it where it sits. The AI Data Engine will now discover metadata across ONTAP, StorageGRID and storage from other vendors, over NFS, SMB and S3. Baxter said the engine held a customer's metadata catalog, and that NetApp customers get the capability at no charge for at least the first six months. Customers had told the company that the earlier version worked only with data on NetApp systems.
"For too long, AI initiatives have depended on complex pipelines that move data away from where it is created, governed, and protected," said Asad Khan, senior vice president and general manager for AI at NetApp.
A widened Commvault integration sends signals from ONTAP's Autonomous Ransomware Protection to the Commvault console. Baxter said independent labs measured 99% accuracy in detecting ransomware, with no false positives in testing. Commvault's Pranay Ahlawat said the integration should reduce mean time to clean recovery.
NetApp Console gains an AI ChatOps interface that connects through an open LLM gateway, so customers can use their own approved models to manage storage. Baxter said a human approves significant actions. Console will also run inside a customer's environment, connected or air-gapped, and NetApp is folding Active IQ Unified Manager into it.
Keystone Sovereign, an entitlement for the company's storage-as-a-service program, starts with qualified customers in the European Economic Area. Baxter said telemetry, logs, backups and support paths stay in the region, and staff who oversee operations are legal residents of it. Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure integration with ONTAP is scheduled for general availability this fall.
In the question period, Jennifer Prenner, senior vice president of product marketing, relayed a question from Victor Ng, editor of Digicon Asia, about sovereignty across nodes. Banerjee said isolation is the core of sovereignty and that ONTAP's multi-tenancy separates departments by access, routing and data management.

NetApp Talks Up SAP Partnership, Stops Short of a Firm Deal
By Martin Holloway29/09/2026No Comments4 Mins Read
NetApp (NTAP) said on 29 September 2026 it intends to expand its long-standing NetApp SAP partnership, with plans to explore deeper integration of its storage tools into SAP Cloud Infrastructure, SAP SE (SAP)’s infrastructure-as-a-service platform.
The release contains no financial figure, no contract term and no timeline. It describes an “intent” to “explore” – language that falls well short of a signed deal.
What the NetApp SAP partnership announcement actually says
NTAP over the last month, hourly closes. Source: consolidated US exchange data.
NetApp’s statement says its platform already supports “key elements” of SAP Cloud Infrastructure’s storage architecture, including file and block storage services. The company frames the new step as evaluating NetApp Object storage and joint go-to-market work, according to the release carried on Business Wire and picked up independently by Investing.com, which reported the same executive framing.
Buried in the full text of the release is a disclaimer stating the plans “do not constitute a commitment, obligation, guarantee, or warranty of any kind by NetApp, including about availability, functionality, pricing, or timing”, according to the complete version published by StockTitan. That clause sits at odds with headline language describing an “expanded partnership”.
NetApp’s underlying relationship with SAP is not new. The company’s own marketing material cites more than two decades of infrastructure collaboration, including work underpinning SAP’s HANA Enterprise Cloud. Tuesday’s announcement adds a further exploratory layer to that history rather than establishing it from scratch.
Material definitive agreements typically trigger an 8-K filing. None accompanies this announcement. NetApp’s most recent 8-K filings in the period relate solely to its fiscal first-quarter results, filed on 2 September 2026, according to SEC EDGAR. SAP has not issued its own confirming statement referenced in the pack.
The SAP item also arrived as one of several NetApp announcements issued the same day around its INSIGHT 2026 conference, including a separate and more concrete tie-up with Oracle to launch a fully managed cloud storage service, according to StockTitan‘s coverage of the conference slate. That clustering makes it hard to credit any single announcement, including the SAP one, with moving sentiment on its own.
Netapp, Inc. revenue by quarter, as filed. Source: SEC EDGAR.
NetApp shares closed at $208.28 as of 18:00 UTC on 29 September, up 1.97% on the day and 10.17% over the prior 20 trading sessions, touching a 20-day high on the same session, according to consolidated US exchange data. Trading volume ran below the 20-day average, at 0.81 times the norm, suggesting the move was not driven by unusually heavy turnover.
With the Oracle deal, INSIGHT 2026 product sessions and the SAP statement all landing together, isolating the market’s reaction to any one item is not possible from the public record. A Form 4 filed for NetApp chief executive George Kurian on 28 September, the day before the announcements, is unrelated routine reporting rather than a signal tied to the SAP news, according to SEC EDGAR.
NetApp’s most recent quarterly results, covering the period to 31 July 2026, showed net income of $375m on revenue of $2,025m, according to the company’s 10-Q filing with the SEC. Diluted earnings per share for the quarter came to $1.88, up from $1.15 a year earlier. None of that quarter’s results reference SAP specifically; they provide context on a company that has posted steadily rising profitability over the past several quarters rather than a read on the new partnership language.
For now, the SAP relationship remains where NetApp’s release leaves it: an intent to explore, not an agreement to deliver. Investors watching for a firmer signal would need to see either a joint statement from SAP itself or a subsequent filing describing binding commercial terms, neither of which has surfaced since the announcement.

Why Is NetApp (NTAP) Up 16% Since Last Earnings Report?
It has been about a month since the last earnings report for NetApp (NTAP). Shares have added about 16% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.
But investors have to be wondering, will the recent positive trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is NetApp due for a pullback? Well, first let's take a quick look at its latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the recent drivers for NetApp, Inc. before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late.
NetApp delivered a record first quarter of fiscal 2027, with non-GAAP earnings of $2.58 per share, up 66.5% year over year. The figure beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $2.13 by 21.1%.
Net revenues rose 29.9% to $2,025 million and surpassed the $1,843 million consensus mark by 9.9%. Strong AI and modernization spending, accelerated purchases and pricing benefits supported growth. Billings increased 36.1% to $2,057 million.
Hybrid Cloud revenues advanced 30.1% year over year to $1,819 million. Product revenues climbed 50.9% to $987 million, while support revenues increased 11.3% to $720 million. Professional and Other Services revenues rose 15.5% to $112 million, mainly on continued Keystone growth.
The quarter included an additional week, which contributed approximately $65 million to revenues, mainly from support and Public Cloud. Excluding that benefit, total revenues increased 26% year over year. Management also cited a healthier demand environment as customers invested in AI and infrastructure modernization.
Flash and Public Cloud Momentum Accelerates
All-flash array revenues reached a record $1,309 million, up 46.6% from the prior-year quarter. Hybrid-flash and other revenues were $510 million versus $505 million a year ago. Together, all-flash and Public Cloud represented 75% of quarterly net revenues.
Public Cloud revenues grew 28% to a record $206 million, reflecting strong first-party and marketplace storage demand. Adjusted for the extra week, Public Cloud growth was 19%. NetApp won approximately 350 AI and data lake modernization deals, with management noting larger deal sizes as customers moved from pilots to production. The company also acquired DataPelago to expand its AI data infrastructure capabilities.
Non-GAAP gross margin was 70.6%, down 50 basis points year over year. The decline reflected a larger product mix, with product revenues accounting for 49% of sales versus 42% a year earlier. Product gross margin was 54.6%, pressured sequentially by higher component costs but partly offset by better pricing.
Hybrid Cloud gross margin was 68.8%, while Public Cloud gross margin reached 86.4%. Support gross margin totaled 93.2%, and Professional Services gross margin was 36.6%. Year-over-year margin expansion across product, support, Professional Services and Public Cloud partly offset the product-mix headwind.
Non-GAAP operating expenses rose 10.9% year over year to $784 million, driven primarily by variable compensation and the additional week, which added approximately $22 million. Even so, non-GAAP operating income increased 60.8% to $645 million.
The non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 31.9% from 25.7%. Non-GAAP net income increased 64% to $515 million. On a GAAP basis, net income rose 60.9% to $375 million, while earnings increased 63.5% to $1.88 per share.
Cash from operations fell 25.3% year over year to $503 million, while free cash flow declined 35.3% to $401 million. Free cash flow margin was 19.8% compared with 39.8% a year ago. Capital expenditures increased to $102 million from $53 million.
NTAP ended the quarter with $3.58 billion in cash, cash equivalents and investments and $2.49 billion in gross debt, leaving net cash of $1.09 billion. Inventory increased to $375 million from $198 million at fiscal year-end as the company managed supply levels to support growing demand. NetApp returned $302 million through $200 million of repurchases and $102 million of dividends.
For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, NetApp expects revenues of $2.025-$2.175 billion. Non-GAAP gross margin is projected at 67-68%, operating margin at 30.9-31.9% and earnings at $2.54-$2.64 per share. Management expects the sequential gross-margin decline mainly from a higher product revenue mix.
For fiscal 2027, revenues are now forecast at $7.975-$8.225 billion, with the $8.10 billion midpoint representing 17% growth and a $650 million increase from prior guidance. Non-GAAP gross margin is expected at 68.1-69.1%, operating margin at 30.3-31.3% and earnings at $9.73-$10.03 per share. The $9.88 earnings midpoint represents 22% year-over-year growth.
How Have Estimates Been Moving Since Then?

NetApp Q1 Earnings Call: AI, Cloud Power Outlook
Tipranks - Tipranks - Wed Sep 16, 7:06PM CDT
NetApp Inc ((NTAP)) has held its Q1 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.
NetApp’s latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone, underscoring record quarterly results and strong demand for its storage and cloud offerings. Management acknowledged some margin pressure from product mix and higher component costs, but emphasized powerful AI and cloud momentum, robust cash generation, and enough confidence to materially raise full-year and fiscal 2027 guidance.
NetApp delivered a record-setting first quarter that surpassed guidance on every key metric, signaling strong operational execution. Revenue jumped 30% year-over-year to $2.03 billion, gross profit climbed 29% to a record $1.43 billion, operating margin reached 31.9%, and non-GAAP EPS surged 66% to $2.58.
Demand was described as broad-based, spanning customer sizes, geographies, industries, and workloads, both on-premises and in cloud. Management attributed the strength to a healthier IT spending environment as customers invest in AI and modernization, with some help from accelerated purchases and pricing tailwinds.
All-flash array revenue hit $1.31 billion in the quarter, up 47% year-over-year and a clear highlight for investors focused on high-performance storage. Executives said customers are standardizing on NetApp for mission-critical and GPU-intensive AI pipelines, pointing to innovation and sales execution as drivers of share gains.
Public cloud revenue grew 28% year-over-year to $206 million, or 19% after adjusting for the extra week in the quarter. Adoption of first-party and marketplace storage services was the key catalyst, and public cloud gross margin reached 86.4%, improving 70 basis points sequentially and more than six points versus last year.
Hybrid Cloud and Product Revenue Expansion
Hybrid Cloud revenue rose to $1.82 billion, up 30% year-over-year and 27% excluding the extra week, highlighting NetApp’s strength in blended environments. Product revenue climbed 51% to $987 million, and management noted accelerating interest in hybrid-flash solutions as customers balance performance and cost.
NetApp closed about 350 AI and data lake modernization deals in the quarter, down from roughly 500 previously but with much larger deal sizes. Management said customers are shifting from proofs of concept to production-level AI workloads, with earlier wins expanding into full-scale environments.
The company highlighted several marquee AI platform deals, including a major agreement with Samsung Electronics that showcases NetApp’s role in advanced data infrastructure. Additional wins included a significant public-sector modernization project using AFX with NVIDIA SuperPOD and a deal with an Asian neo-cloud provider for secure, scalable AI storage.
New Customers and Competitive Displacements
New customer counts, spending from new logos, and expansion within the existing base all came in ahead of internal plans, signaling healthy commercial traction. Examples ranged from a major U.S. utility standardizing on NetApp’s AI-ready infrastructure to a European IT service provider and a competitive displacement at a leading transportation agency.
NetApp reported strong wins around Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Azure NetApp Files as enterprises migrate VMware and modernize data across clouds. Management emphasized that these offerings delivered better performance, lower cost, and broad workload support, translating into meaningful savings in highlighted deployments.
The acquisition of DataPelago brings Nucleus, a software engine focused on high-performance in-place data processing that reduces the need to move data. NetApp said the technology enhances its AI data infrastructure capabilities and helps customers unlock additional value from unstructured data already stored on its platforms.
At the start of the second quarter, NetApp closed the purchase of JetStream, a specialist in cloud-native disaster recovery for VMware environments. JetStream enables continuous protection and recovery across diverse storage setups with replication to NetApp cloud offerings, including Azure NetApp Files.
Recurring Revenue and Contract Visibility
The company exited Q1 with $4.85 billion in deferred revenue, up 7% year-over-year, signaling durable recurring streams. Remaining performance obligations rose 14% to $5.65 billion, giving NetApp sizable visibility into future contracted revenue.
Operating income rose 61% to $645 million, with operating margin expanding 6.1 points to 31.9%, highlighting strong operating leverage. Cash flow from operations reached $503 million and free cash flow was $401 million, underscoring the business’s ability to convert earnings into cash.
Shareholder Returns and Reduced Share Count
NetApp returned $302 million to shareholders in the quarter, split between $200 million in buybacks and $102 million in dividends. Diluted share count fell by 3 million shares, or 1.5% year-over-year, enhancing EPS and signaling ongoing commitment to capital returns.
The company ended the quarter with $3.6 billion in cash and short-term investments versus $2.5 billion in gross debt. That left NetApp in a net cash position of $1.1 billion, providing ample financial flexibility for investment, acquisitions, and shareholder returns.
Professional Services revenue climbed 15% year-over-year to $112 million, driven largely by continued expansion of the Keystone subscription business. Management said Keystone growth was in line with prior quarters and the broader flash portfolio, with more new customers and added capabilities.
NetApp is leaning into AI by continuing to invest in new solutions while keeping a tight rein on operating expenses. Executives reiterated that expected full-year operating expense growth will be well below projected revenue growth, supporting margin expansion.
AFX is being positioned as a high-end solution for performance and scale, especially in AI GPU-as-a-service setups, neo-clouds, and private AI clouds. Management said AFX is going through certifications at a large number of customers and is making solid progress in these demanding environments.
Overall gross margin came in at 70.6%, down 50 basis points year-over-year, reflecting a heavier mix of product revenue. Products represented 49% of total revenue versus 42% a year earlier, boosting top-line growth but exerting pressure on margins.
Higher Component Costs Hit Product Margins
Product gross margin was 54.6%, down 150 basis points sequentially, mainly due to higher component costs even as pricing improved. Management expects to recoup some of the incremental costs over time but cautioned that product margins are unlikely to stay at Q1’s elevated levels.
For the second quarter, NetApp anticipates gross margin of 67% to 68%, lower sequentially as product revenue is expected to make up a larger share of the mix. The guidance reflects management’s view that strong hardware demand will continue to trade off against blended margin levels.
Inventory expanded both year-over-year and sequentially as NetApp secured components to support rising demand and managed supply-chain risk. Inventory turns slipped to six, indicating the company is holding more stock to stay ahead of growth and potential constraints.
AI and data lake deal count fell from about 500 to roughly 350 quarter-over-quarter, a metric that may catch investors’ eyes. Management stressed that the shift reflects fewer, larger production deals rather than weakening demand, as existing proof-of-concept projects scale up.
Purchase Timing Shifts by Customer Priority
Executives noted some large customers accelerated certain high-priority projects into a single quarter instead of spreading them out. At the same time, some lower-priority purchases were moderated or deferred, introducing timing variability but not changing the overall demand outlook.
For Q2, NetApp expects revenue around $2.1 billion, plus or minus $75 million, implying 23% growth at the midpoint, with gross margin of 67% to 68% and operating margin of roughly 31%. Looking to fiscal 2027, the company raised guidance to $7.975 billion to $8.225 billion in revenue and EPS between $9.73 and $10.03, targeting high-teens growth and solid profitability.
NetApp’s earnings call painted the picture of a company riding strong AI and cloud trends while managing through predictable margin trade-offs. NetApp Inc. (ISIN US64120B1098) stock is trading near its recent highs after the data storage specialist reported record fiscal first quarter 2027 results, with revenue rising 30.0 percent year over year to USD 2.02 billion and adjusted EPS jumping 66.0 percent to USD 2.58 as of Q1 fiscal 2027, according to Zacks on September 8, 2026.
Strong Q1 figures and higher fiscal 2027 guidance
NetApp delivered what it described as record results for its fiscal first quarter 2027, with Q1 revenue of USD 2.02 billion compared with market expectations of around USD 1.84 billion, beating consensus by nearly 10 percent as reported by Zacks on September 8, 2026.
On the bottom line, NetApp's adjusted EPS for Q1 fiscal 2027 reached USD 2.58, up 66 percent from the prior-year quarter and well ahead of analyst expectations of USD 2.13, marking a roughly 21 percent outperformance versus consensus according to Zacks on September 8, 2026.
Reflecting this momentum, management significantly raised its fiscal 2027 guidance, now expecting revenue between USD 7.98 billion and USD 8.23 billion and adjusted EPS in a range of USD 9.73 to USD 10.03, up from earlier targets as noted by Zacks on September 8, 2026.
AI and cloud demand support the story, but risks remain
Beyond the headline numbers, NetApp emphasized AI and cloud infrastructure trends as key drivers of its outlook at recent industry conferences. At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia plus Technology Conference 2026, the company described a strong start to fiscal 2027 and highlighted that AI workloads and cloud storage demand are lifting its pipeline, according to Investing.com on September 8, 2026.
At Citi's 2026 Global TMT Conference on September 8, 2026, NetApp reiterated that demand remained strong across its business, supported by AI adoption and infrastructure modernization, while repeating that fiscal first quarter 2027 revenue exceeded guidance across the board, as reported by Investing.com on September 8, 2026.
Management also acknowledged headwinds such as higher component costs, supply tightness and intense competition in storage and data management, suggesting that maintaining margins will require careful pricing and product differentiation, according to Investing.com on September 8, 2026.
Analyst view and valuation metrics around the consensus target
The strong quarter and raised guidance have reinforced positive analyst sentiment, but valuation is becoming a discussion point. NetApp currently carries a consensus rating of Hold across 16 analysts, with 6 Buy ratings and 10 Hold ratings and an average price target of USD 192.07, according to MarketBeat on September 8, 2026.
The same overview from MarketBeat on September 8, 2026 shows a high price target of USD 219.00 and a low target of USD 150.00 for NetApp, implying potential upside of about 1.6 percent from the average target versus the latest trading levels.
Zacks highlighted NetApp as one of its Investment Ideas on September 8, 2026, noting that both NetApp and networking firm Ciena crushed quarterly earnings expectations and raised their outlooks, and assigning NetApp a Zacks Rank number 2 (Buy) based on favorable earnings estimate revisions, according to Zacks on September 8, 2026.
At the same time, a detailed post-earnings analysis from Charged Alpha's Stock Encyclopedia argued that NetApp's 29.9 percent reported revenue growth in Q1 fiscal 2027 relies partly on a 53-week fiscal year and pricing effects, estimating underlying growth closer to 20.6 percent when adjusted for the extra week, and noting that free cash flow fell 35 percent to USD 401 million even as net income rose 61 percent, according to Charged Alpha Stock Encyclopedia on September 9, 2026.
For income-oriented investors, NetApp continues to offer a modest dividend yield. Recent institutional filings compiled by MarketBeat on September 9, 2026 note that NetApp declared a quarterly dividend of USD 0.52 per share, corresponding to an annualized payout of USD 2.08 and a yield around 1.1 percent based on recent prices, with a payout ratio of roughly 29.34 percent.
The same set of filings shows active trading in the shareholder base, with California State Teachers Retirement System reported as buying NetApp shares and asset manager Amundi reported as selling holdings, according to separate institutional alerts from MarketBeat and MarketBeat both dated September 9, 2026, underlining that large investors are actively repositioning around the stock after the strong quarter.
Another filing summary from MarketBeat on September 9, 2026 reports that Empirical Finance LLC acquired 5,617 NetApp shares, further illustrating institutional appetite following the latest earnings release and guidance update.
Stock performance and valuation as of early September 2026
As of September 8, 2026, NetApp shares traded in a daily range between USD 182.53 and USD 190.21 on Nasdaq, with a market capitalization of around USD 37.15 billion and a trailing price-earnings ratio of approximately 26.68, according to price data from MarketBeat updated on September 8, 2026.

NetApp Unveils Novus, AI Data Engine Upgrades to Power Agentic AI
Interested in NetApp, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.
NetApp unveiled Novus, a disaggregated storage architecture designed for large AI factories and GPU clusters exceeding 100,000 GPUs, with claimed performance of up to 100 TB per second and a zettabyte-scale file system.
The company expanded its AI Data Engine to discover and activate heterogeneous enterprise data across storage systems and clouds without requiring migration. NetApp will offer the platform and new metadata capabilities free for the first six months.
NetApp also introduced broader hybrid-cloud management, security and recovery tools, while expanding partnerships with Oracle Cloud, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure to support enterprise and sovereign AI workloads.
5 Tech Stocks Holding Their Ground Through the AI Trade Pullback
NetApp (NASDAQ:NTAP) used its INSIGHT 2026 event to outline a strategy for helping enterprises prepare data infrastructure for agentic AI, announcing expanded cloud partnerships, enhancements to its AI Data Engine and management platform, and a new high-scale storage architecture called NetApp Novus.
George Kurian said organizations seeking to move AI projects from pilot programs into production face two core issues: infrastructure constraints and difficulty harnessing fragmented enterprise data. He said AI systems require increasingly large GPU clusters and datasets, while unstructured information remains dispersed across storage systems, clouds, remote offices and sovereignty jurisdictions.
→ Advanced Micro Devices Is Spending $8.2 Billion to Learn What AI Needs Next
Is Backblaze the Next Momentum Monster?
"Data is becoming the constraint to productively scale AI," Kurian said. He cited NetApp's view that 93% of organizations report at least one data challenge blocking their AI ambitions.
AI Data Engine expands beyond NetApp data
Syam Nair, NetApp's Chief Product Officer, said the company's platform is intended to provide AI-ready data, proactive protection, unified storage and complete control across hybrid environments. He said the goal is to activate data where it resides rather than require customers to copy or migrate it.
→ JPMorgan Bets on Genius Sports as the Market Loses Patience
Semtech Stock Climbs as AI Boom Drives Turnaround Success
Nair announced that the metadata capability of the NetApp AI Data Engine will support heterogeneous data sources, extending beyond NetApp-managed data. The software-defined capability is designed to discover, understand and activate data across an enterprise estate without moving it into another system, according to Nair.
NetApp said it will make the AI Data Engine and its new metadata capability available free for the first six months. Nair said the platform is intended to surface data patterns and context while applying governance and protection policies.
→ AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird Progress Comes With Several Risks Still Unresolved
The company also highlighted its acquisition of DataPelago. Nair said DataPelago is designed to accelerate existing tools used by researchers and data teams, including Spark, Trino and Python libraries, within the data infrastructure and without code changes.
Security, recovery and hybrid management
Nair said NetApp is pursuing what it calls "zero trust data security," with protection built into data rather than centered solely on network posture or identity checks. He said AI readiness and data protection must operate together because autonomous agents could act on compromised information at machine speed.
NetApp also described expanded integration with Commvault. According to Nair, potential ransomware attacks will be surfaced within the Commvault interface, while NetApp's SnapRestore and curated clean recovery capabilities will support recovery workflows.
For hybrid infrastructure management, the company introduced the NetApp Console, which Nair described as a control plane for on-premises systems, Keystone and major public clouds. The console includes AI-assisted operations intended to predict issues, resolve incidents and optimize capacity and costs with human oversight.
NetApp said the console can also operate in local, air-gapped environments. Nair said existing Active IQ Unified Manager customers will have an upgrade path rather than need to replace their management tooling.
The company additionally unveiled Keystone Sovereign, an add-on entitlement for Keystone subscriptions aimed at European Economic Area customers with regional compliance and data-residency requirements. Nair said the offering will be available in early November for France and Germany, followed by broader availability later.
Mahesh Thiagarajan, executive vice president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle, said Oracle and NetApp are partnering to bring ONTAP to OCI. He said OCI File Storage and NetApp ONTAP will soon enable customers to run business-critical file-storage workloads in OCI using ONTAP tools, APIs and automation.
Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said Google Cloud NetApp Volumes supports enterprise workloads, agentic workloads and retrieval-augmented generation inferencing. He also said NetApp storage solutions are now embedded natively in Google Distributed Cloud, supporting air-gapped sovereign environments for Google AI models.
Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Microsoft Cloud, said Microsoft and NetApp continue to help customers bring ONTAP workloads to Azure and run demanding workloads through Azure NetApp Files.
NetApp introduces Novus for AI factories
The event's largest announcement was NetApp Novus, a new disaggregated architecture intended for accelerated computing environments, large AI factories and GPU clusters exceeding 100,000 GPUs.
Kurian said Novus is designed to independently scale storage components and assimilate data across tens of thousands of systems into a single namespace. NetApp said the architecture is designed to deliver up to 100 TB per second of performance and a zettabyte-scale file system, claims the company characterized as first-of-their-kind capabilities.
Arindam Banerjee, NetApp's Chief Platform and Technology Officer, said Novus uses federation to combine multiple storage clusters into one namespace, with throughput increasing as clusters are added. The architecture uses standard pNFS and Flex Files protocols, he said, allowing use of the stock Linux kernel rather than requiring a proprietary client or kernel module.
Banerjee said Novus separates metadata services into independently scalable protocol, state and catalog planes, addressing metadata bottlenecks that can arise when AI workloads combine high-volume data reads and writes with extensive metadata operations. Novus data servers will run ONTAP, he added, extending NetApp's existing data integrity, resilience, security, isolation and quality-of-service capabilities to the new architecture.
Kurian said the announcements reflect NetApp's effort to help customers build intelligent data infrastructure that can transform enterprise data into usable knowledge for AI systems and agents.
NetApp, Inc develops intelligent data infrastructure and data management solutions for enterprises, service providers, and government organizations. The company helps customers store, manage, protect, and access data across on-premises environments, private clouds, public clouds, and hybrid multicloud infrastructures.
Its portfolio includes enterprise storage systems, all-flash arrays, cloud-connected storage, object storage, and data management software. NetApp's offerings include the ONTAP data management operating system, AFF and ASA storage systems, StorageGRID object storage, and BlueXP, a platform designed to help customers manage data and storage resources across multiple environments.

NetApp Unveils AI Storage Architecture, Oracle Cloud Service And Agent Controls
NetApp announces its Novus AI storage architecture, Oracle Cloud Storage Service and updates to its AI data platform, security and sovereignty controls.
NetApp announced a storage architecture for AI data centers, a storage service with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and updates to its data platform Wednesday. The company framed the products around one problem: AI agents act on enterprise data at machine speed, while the infrastructure underneath was not built for that pace.
The centerpiece is NetApp Novus, an architecture that NetApp says is designed to exceed throughput of 100 terabytes per second and support hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Arindam Banerjee, NetApp's chief platform and technology officer, said storage stopped limiting applications years ago because those applications ran on CPUs. GPUs changed the equation, and new GPU generations arrive every 12 months.
Banerjee said market studies showed GPU utilization as low as 5% at some deployments. The company's press release puts the figure below 30% for storage designs that predate AI factories. Banerjee described the arithmetic behind the target: 50,000 GPUs, each drawing 2 gigabytes per second, add up to 100 terabytes per second from one namespace.
Novus separates metadata from the data path. Banerjee said the two run on separate nodes, so the lookups agents generate do not compete with large reads. Clients learn where data is placed and go to the right node for each task. The initial releases pair Novus Data Director, the metadata software, with ONTAP data services on AFF A90 systems, running on Supermicro infrastructure that NetApp has qualified. The system uses NFS and the pNFS flex files standard. Banerjee said competitors at this scale need a custom client to route traffic.
He gave figures to support the scaling claim. NetApp builds in blocks of 1 terabyte per second, added one at a time, in the manner of hyperscaler designs. A lab system at 10 terabytes per second runs today, he said, with linear scaling. Reaching 100 terabytes per second would take a federation of about 1,250 nodes. He said Google's managed Lustre announcement at Google Next reached 10 terabytes per second. He also said NetApp's internal tests reached 70,000 file creates per second.
Tony Palmer, chief analyst at Omdia, said the firm audited Novus and saw near-linear scaling as ONTAP clusters were added to the namespace. Omdia's modeling projects 100 TBps for sequential reads with dozens of exabytes of capacity. Novus is orderable today, and NetApp says software-defined deployments will follow.
NetApp and Oracle said they will launch Oracle Cloud Infrastructure NetApp Storage Service, a managed service that brings ONTAP data management to OCI. Customers will manage it through the OCI Console and SDKs, ONTAP APIs and existing operational workflows. General availability is planned within 12 months.
Jeff Baxter, NetApp's vice president of technical marketing, said the service will be an Oracle product built on ONTAP software. He noted that Azure NetApp Files, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Google Cloud NetApp Volumes already exist, which makes Oracle the fourth of the largest clouds to carry a first-party ONTAP offering.
"Enterprises shouldn't have to rebuild their data infrastructure to move to the cloud," said Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
Baxter opened the briefing with a Gartner projection that 40% of enterprise applications will embed task-specific AI agents this year and that agents will handle 15% of daily business decisions by 2028. He said cost per token becomes the constraint as adoption grows.
NetApp's answer on data is to leave it where it sits. The AI Data Engine will now discover metadata across ONTAP, StorageGRID and storage from other vendors, over NFS, SMB and S3. Baxter said the engine held a customer's metadata catalog, and that NetApp customers get the capability at no charge for at least the first six months. Customers had told the company that the earlier version worked only with data on NetApp systems.
"For too long, AI initiatives have depended on complex pipelines that move data away from where it is created, governed, and protected," said Asad Khan, senior vice president and general manager for AI at NetApp.
A widened Commvault integration sends signals from ONTAP's Autonomous Ransomware Protection to the Commvault console. Baxter said independent labs measured 99% accuracy in detecting ransomware, with no false positives in testing. Commvault's Pranay Ahlawat said the integration should reduce mean time to clean recovery.
NetApp Console gains an AI ChatOps interface that connects through an open LLM gateway, so customers can use their own approved models to manage storage. Baxter said a human approves significant actions. Console will also run inside a customer's environment, connected or air-gapped, and NetApp is folding Active IQ Unified Manager into it.
Keystone Sovereign, an entitlement for the company's storage-as-a-service program, starts with qualified customers in the European Economic Area. Baxter said telemetry, logs, backups and support paths stay in the region, and staff who oversee operations are legal residents of it. Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure integration with ONTAP is scheduled for general availability this fall.
In the question period, Jennifer Prenner, senior vice president of product marketing, relayed a question from Victor Ng, editor of Digicon Asia, about sovereignty across nodes. Banerjee said isolation is the core of sovereignty and that ONTAP's multi-tenancy separates departments by access, routing and data management.

NetApp Talks Up SAP Partnership, Stops Short of a Firm Deal
By Martin Holloway29/09/2026No Comments4 Mins Read
NetApp (NTAP) said on 29 September 2026 it intends to expand its long-standing NetApp SAP partnership, with plans to explore deeper integration of its storage tools into SAP Cloud Infrastructure, SAP SE (SAP)’s infrastructure-as-a-service platform.
The release contains no financial figure, no contract term and no timeline. It describes an “intent” to “explore” – language that falls well short of a signed deal.
What the NetApp SAP partnership announcement actually says
NTAP over the last month, hourly closes. Source: consolidated US exchange data.
NetApp’s statement says its platform already supports “key elements” of SAP Cloud Infrastructure’s storage architecture, including file and block storage services. The company frames the new step as evaluating NetApp Object storage and joint go-to-market work, according to the release carried on Business Wire and picked up independently by Investing.com, which reported the same executive framing.
Buried in the full text of the release is a disclaimer stating the plans “do not constitute a commitment, obligation, guarantee, or warranty of any kind by NetApp, including about availability, functionality, pricing, or timing”, according to the complete version published by StockTitan. That clause sits at odds with headline language describing an “expanded partnership”.
NetApp’s underlying relationship with SAP is not new. The company’s own marketing material cites more than two decades of infrastructure collaboration, including work underpinning SAP’s HANA Enterprise Cloud. Tuesday’s announcement adds a further exploratory layer to that history rather than establishing it from scratch.
Material definitive agreements typically trigger an 8-K filing. None accompanies this announcement. NetApp’s most recent 8-K filings in the period relate solely to its fiscal first-quarter results, filed on 2 September 2026, according to SEC EDGAR. SAP has not issued its own confirming statement referenced in the pack.
The SAP item also arrived as one of several NetApp announcements issued the same day around its INSIGHT 2026 conference, including a separate and more concrete tie-up with Oracle to launch a fully managed cloud storage service, according to StockTitan‘s coverage of the conference slate. That clustering makes it hard to credit any single announcement, including the SAP one, with moving sentiment on its own.
Netapp, Inc. revenue by quarter, as filed. Source: SEC EDGAR.
NetApp shares closed at $208.28 as of 18:00 UTC on 29 September, up 1.97% on the day and 10.17% over the prior 20 trading sessions, touching a 20-day high on the same session, according to consolidated US exchange data. Trading volume ran below the 20-day average, at 0.81 times the norm, suggesting the move was not driven by unusually heavy turnover.
With the Oracle deal, INSIGHT 2026 product sessions and the SAP statement all landing together, isolating the market’s reaction to any one item is not possible from the public record. A Form 4 filed for NetApp chief executive George Kurian on 28 September, the day before the announcements, is unrelated routine reporting rather than a signal tied to the SAP news, according to SEC EDGAR.
NetApp’s most recent quarterly results, covering the period to 31 July 2026, showed net income of $375m on revenue of $2,025m, according to the company’s 10-Q filing with the SEC. Diluted earnings per share for the quarter came to $1.88, up from $1.15 a year earlier. None of that quarter’s results reference SAP specifically; they provide context on a company that has posted steadily rising profitability over the past several quarters rather than a read on the new partnership language.
For now, the SAP relationship remains where NetApp’s release leaves it: an intent to explore, not an agreement to deliver. Investors watching for a firmer signal would need to see either a joint statement from SAP itself or a subsequent filing describing binding commercial terms, neither of which has surfaced since the announcement.

Management acknowledged some margin pressure from product mix and higher component costs, but emphasized powerful AI and cloud momentum, robust cash generation, and enough confidence to materially raise full-year and fiscal 2027 guidance.
NetApp delivered a record-setting first quarter that surpassed guidance on every key metric, signaling strong operational execution. Revenue jumped 30% year-over-year to $2.03 billion, gross profit climbed 29% to a record $1.43 billion, operating margin reached 31.9%, and non-GAAP EPS surged 66% to $2.58.
Demand was described as broad-based, spanning customer sizes, geographies, industries, and workloads, both on-premises and in cloud. Management attributed the strength to a healthier IT spending environment as customers invest in AI and modernization, with some help from accelerated purchases and pricing tailwinds.
All-flash array revenue hit $1.31 billion in the quarter, up 47% year-over-year and a clear highlight for investors focused on high-performance storage. Executives said customers are standardizing on NetApp for mission-critical and GPU-intensive AI pipelines, pointing to innovation and sales execution as drivers of share gains.
Public cloud revenue grew 28% year-over-year to $206 million, or 19% after adjusting for the extra week in the quarter. Adoption of first-party and marketplace storage services was the key catalyst, and public cloud gross margin reached 86.4%, improving 70 basis points sequentially and more than six points versus last year.
Hybrid Cloud and Product Revenue Expansion
Hybrid Cloud revenue rose to $1.82 billion, up 30% year-over-year and 27% excluding the extra week, highlighting NetApp’s strength in blended environments. Product revenue climbed 51% to $987 million, and management noted accelerating interest in hybrid-flash solutions as customers balance performance and cost.
NetApp closed about 350 AI and data lake modernization deals in the quarter, down from roughly 500 previously but with much larger deal sizes. Management said customers are shifting from proofs of concept to production-level AI workloads, with earlier wins expanding into full-scale environments.
The company highlighted several marquee AI platform deals, including a major agreement with Samsung Electronics that showcases NetApp’s role in advanced data infrastructure. Additional wins included a significant public-sector modernization project using AFX with NVIDIA SuperPOD and a deal with an Asian neo-cloud provider for secure, scalable AI storage.
New Customers and Competitive Displacements
New customer counts, spending from new logos, and expansion within the existing base all came in ahead of internal plans, signaling healthy commercial traction. Examples ranged from a major U.S. utility standardizing on NetApp’s AI-ready infrastructure to a European IT service provider and a competitive displacement at a leading transportation agency.
NetApp reported strong wins around Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and Azure NetApp Files as enterprises migrate VMware and modernize data across clouds. Management emphasized that these offerings delivered better performance, lower cost, and broad workload support, translating into meaningful savings in highlighted deployments.
The acquisition of DataPelago brings Nucleus, a software engine focused on high-performance in-place data processing that reduces the need to move data. NetApp said the technology enhances its AI data infrastructure capabilities and helps customers unlock additional value from unstructured data already stored on its platforms.
At the start of the second quarter, NetApp closed the purchase of JetStream, a specialist in cloud-native disaster recovery for VMware environments. JetStream enables continuous protection and recovery across diverse storage setups with replication to NetApp cloud offerings, including Azure NetApp Files.
Recurring Revenue and Contract Visibility
The company exited Q1 with $4.85 billion in deferred revenue, up 7% year-over-year, signaling durable recurring streams. Remaining performance obligations rose 14% to $5.65 billion, giving NetApp sizable visibility into future contracted revenue.
Operating income rose 61% to $645 million, with operating margin expanding 6.1 points to 31.9%, highlighting strong operating leverage. Cash flow from operations reached $503 million and free cash flow was $401 million, underscoring the business’s ability to convert earnings into cash.
Shareholder Returns and Reduced Share Count
NetApp returned $302 million to shareholders in the quarter, split between $200 million in buybacks and $102 million in dividends. Diluted share count fell by 3 million shares, or 1.5% year-over-year, enhancing EPS and signaling ongoing commitment to capital returns.
The company ended the quarter with $3.6 billion in cash and short-term investments versus $2.5 billion in gross debt. That left NetApp in a net cash position of $1.1 billion, providing ample financial flexibility for investment, acquisitions, and shareholder returns.
Professional Services revenue climbed 15% year-over-year to $112 million, driven largely by continued expansion of the Keystone subscription business. Management said Keystone growth was in line with prior quarters and the broader flash portfolio, with more new customers and added capabilities.
NetApp is leaning into AI by continuing to invest in new solutions while keeping a tight rein on operating expenses. Executives reiterated that expected full-year operating expense growth will be well below projected revenue growth, supporting margin expansion.
AFX is being positioned as a high-end solution for performance and scale, especially in AI GPU-as-a-service setups, neo-clouds, and private AI clouds. Management said AFX is going through certifications at a large number of customers and is making solid progress in these demanding environments.
Overall gross margin came in at 70.6%, down 50 basis points year-over-year, reflecting a heavier mix of product revenue. Products represented 49% of total revenue versus 42% a year earlier, boosting top-line growth but exerting pressure on margins.
Higher Component Costs Hit Product Margins
Product gross margin was 54.6%, down 150 basis points sequentially, mainly due to higher component costs even as pricing improved. Management expects to recoup some of the incremental costs over time but cautioned that product margins are unlikely to stay at Q1’s elevated levels.
For the second quarter, NetApp anticipates gross margin of 67% to 68%, lower sequentially as product revenue is expected to make up a larger share of the mix. The guidance reflects management’s view that strong hardware demand will continue to trade off against blended margin levels.
Inventory expanded both year-over-year and sequentially as NetApp secured components to support rising demand and managed supply-chain risk. Inventory turns slipped to six, indicating the company is holding more stock to stay ahead of growth and potential constraints.
AI and data lake deal count fell from about 500 to roughly 350 quarter-over-quarter, a metric that may catch investors’ eyes. Management stressed that the shift reflects fewer, larger production deals rather than weakening demand, as existing proof-of-concept projects scale up.
Purchase Timing Shifts by Customer Priority
Executives noted some large customers accelerated certain high-priority projects into a single quarter instead of spreading them out. At the same time, some lower-priority purchases were moderated or deferred, introducing timing variability but not changing the overall demand outlook.
For Q2, NetApp expects revenue around $2.1 billion, plus or minus $75 million, implying 23% growth at the midpoint, with gross margin of 67% to 68% and operating margin of roughly 31%. Looking to fiscal 2027, the company raised guidance to $7.975 billion to $8.225 billion in revenue and EPS between $9.73 and $10.03, targeting high-teens growth and solid profitability.
NetApp’s earnings call painted the picture of a company riding strong AI and cloud trends while managing through predictable margin trade-offs. With record Q1 results, rising recurring revenue, disciplined spending, and higher long-term guidance, the story remains one of growth and cash-generating resilience that will interest investors watching infrastructure and AI plays.

“NetApp delivered a record-setting start to the year, exceeding guidance on every metric and achieving our strongest first quarter ever,” said George Kurian, Chief Executive Officer. “Our momentum reflects not only the trust of existing customers but also our success in winning new ones, as organizations choose the NetApp Platform to power their AI and hybrid multi-cloud initiatives. Through continued innovation and strategic investments, we are enabling customers to address their most critical needs and creating lasting value for all stakeholders.”

First Quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Business Highlights
NetApp announced the release of StorageGRID 12.1, designed to help customers scale AI and other modern workloads with a federated global namespace, improving how data is accessed, processed, and managed across distributed environments to support AI data pipelines.
NetApp announced new capabilities to NetApp Trident software 26.06 that helps Kubernetes platform teams scale workloads, while adding smarter volume placement, non-disruptive iSCSI volume rebalancing, expanded cloud support, and deeper integration for OpenShift Virtualization migrations.
NetApp announced new data management capabilities optimized for Red Hat OpenShift that enable advanced levels of resilience and scale for virtualized environments, on-premises and in the cloud.
NetApp announced Instaclustr for Model Context Protocol (MCP) Gateway, a fully managed gateway service that connects Instaclustr managed data infrastructure to AI applications and agents.
NetApp announced the general availability of Azure NetApp Files support for large files up to 64 TiB on regular volumes to help remove the friction from large-scale migrations, de-risk VMware estate moves, and allow architects to design cleaner, more cost-effective solutions.
NetApp announced the general availability of Azure NetApp Files Object REST API to eliminate complex data pipelines and enable direct access to AI capabilities through standardized interfaces.
NetApp introduced nconnect on Azure VMware Solution, increasing throughput and lowering effective latency under load without adding datastores or hosts.
NetApp announced the general availability of Azure NetApp Files migration assistant to accelerate and simplify migrations of business-critical applications and data to Azure.
NetApp announced a collaboration with Cisco to offer new solutions for secure, scalable, and simplified AI, expanding on the success of FlexPod to support AI adoption across organizations.
NetApp announced an expanded collaboration with Cisco to strengthen defense-in-depth strategies for customers with the new NetApp Splunk Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) playbook.
NetApp announced a deepened global alliance with CGI where NetApp Keystone will power CGI’s block storage solutions within its shared services platform.
NetApp and SK Telecom announced the completion of a joint proof of concept, using NetApp AFX systems with SK Telecom’s Petasus AI Cloud, demonstrating a solution that enables enterprises to scale AI infrastructure in virtualized environments while maintaining high performance.
NetApp and Okestro signed a strategic partnership agreement to jointly develop integrated enterprise AI and disaster recovery infrastructure.
NetApp announced a strategic partnership with Tata Consultancy Services to better help organizations discover, classify, and govern data across locations, reduce the impact of cyber-attacks, speed up recovery times, and provide insights on sensitive data locations and permissions.
NetApp announced its acquisition of DataPelago, Inc., to further enable computing where data is created and stored, accelerating demanding workloads while improving infrastructure efficiency at scale.
NetApp appointed Alvaro Celis as Chief Partner and Ecosystem Officer to lead partner ecosystems, modernize incentive programs, improve partner satisfaction, and drive growth.
NetApp CEO, George Kurian, was named to CRN’s 25 Most Influential Executives of 2026 list, emphasizing his leadership in data storage amid the age of cloud and AI.
NetApp’s AI Data Engine was named as a finalist in CRN’s 2026 Tech Innovator Awards, noting its ability to transform massive unstructured data estates into always-fresh, AI-ready assets with enterprise-grade security, compliance, and operational efficiency.
NetApp was named a Leader in the Forrester WaveTM: Object Storage Solutions, Q2 2026, showcasing our strong fit for large enterprises managing distributed, regulated object estates that want to balance governance and hybrid consistency against the need for AI-native storage services.
NetApp was recognized in The Wall Street Journal’s 2026 Best Companies For The Future list, ranking 60 out of 500 organizations.
NetApp was named as one of the Greatest Workplaces in America, California, and Tech for 2026 by Newsweek, receiving a five-star rating based on a comprehensive worker satisfaction study.
NetApp was named to Time Magazine’s Best Companies of 2026 list, ranking 271 out of 1,000 organizations.
NetApp was named as one of the Best Companies to Work For by U.S. News, highlighting its top work environment.

NetApp Usage of Non-GAAP Financial Information
To supplement NetApp’s condensed consolidated financial statement information presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (GAAP), NetApp provides investors with certain non-GAAP measures, including, but not limited to, historical non-GAAP gross margins, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP operating margins, non-GAAP net income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, free cash flow, billings, and historical and projected non-GAAP earnings per share.
NetApp believes that the presentation of its non-GAAP measures, when shown in conjunction with the corresponding GAAP measures, provides useful information to investors and management regarding financial and business trends relating to its financial condition and results of operations. Non-GAAP financial measures are used to: (1) measure company performance against historical results, (2) facilitate comparisons to our competitors’ operating results, and (3) allow greater transparency with respect to information used by management in financial and operational decision making.
NetApp believes that the presentation of non-GAAP gross margins, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP operating margins, non-GAAP effective tax rate, non-GAAP net income, and non-GAAP earnings per share data provides investors with supplemental metrics that assist in understanding current results and future prospects, earnings and profitability that are complementary to GAAP metrics. Each of these non-GAAP metrics is defined as the applicable GAAP metric adjusted to exclude the items defined in A through I below, as applicable, while our non-GAAP effective tax rate and non-GAAP net income also reflect a non-GAAP tax provision, as described in item J below, instead of our GAAP tax provision. GAAP earnings per share and non-GAAP earnings per share are calculated using the net income divided by the diluted number of shares for the applicable period.
NetApp believes that the presentation of free cash flow, which it defines as the net cash provided by operating activities less cash used to acquire property and equipment, to be a liquidity measure that provides useful information to investors and management because it reflects cash that can be used to, among other things, invest in its business, make strategic acquisitions, repurchase common stock, and pay dividends on its common stock. As free cash flow is not a measure of liquidity calculated in accordance with GAAP, free cash flow should be considered in addition to, but not as a substitute for, the analysis provided in the statement of cash flows.
NetApp approximates billings by adding net revenues as reported on our Condensed Consolidated Statements of Operations for the period to the change in total deferred revenue as reported on our Condensed Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows for the same period. Billings is a performance measure that NetApp believes provides useful information to investors and management because it approximates the amounts under purchase orders received by us during a given period that have been billed.

A. Amortization of intangible assets. NetApp records amortization of intangible assets that were acquired in connection with its business combinations. Management finds it useful to exclude these charges to assess the appropriate level of various operating expenses to assist in budgeting, planning and forecasting future periods and in measuring operational performance.
B. Stock-based compensation expenses. NetApp excludes stock-based compensation expenses from its non-GAAP measures primarily because the amount can fluctuate based on variables unrelated to the performance of the underlying business. While management views stock-based compensation as a key element of our employee retention and long-term incentives, we do not view it as an expense to be used in evaluating operational performance in any given period.

NetApp (ISIN US64120B1098) received a higher valuation marker on September 30, 2026, when BofA Securities raised its price target from USD 200.00 to USD 220.00 while retaining a Neutral rating, according to Investing.com. The move puts artificial intelligence demand and NetApp's expanding data-infrastructure opportunity at the center of the valuation debate. BofA based the higher target on a 21-times multiple of estimated calendar 2027 earnings per share, up from a 19-times multiple, the report said. The same account cited a projected expansion in NetApp's total addressable market from USD 20.00 billion today to USD 40.00 billion in three years. The valuation call follows NetApp's first-quarter report, rather than a new quarterly release on October 1, 2026. The September 30 target change is therefore the latest dated analyst event in the stock's current news cycle. According to NetApp in its September 2, 2026 release, GAAP net revenue reached USD 2.03 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with USD 1.56 billion in the year-earlier quarter. That was a 30.00 percent year-over-year increase, while GAAP net income rose to USD 375.00 million from USD 233.00 million. GAAP diluted earnings per share increased to USD 1.88 from USD 1.15 in the same period. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached USD 2.58, compared with USD 1.55 a year earlier, and operating cash flow was USD 503.00 million. NetApp's fiscal 2027 outlook calls for revenue of USD 7.98 billion to USD 8.23 billion and non-GAAP earnings per share of USD 9.73 to USD 10.03. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027, the company guided to revenue of USD 2.03 billion to USD 2.18 billion and non-GAAP earnings per share of USD 2.54 to USD 2.64, according to NetApp. The business mix adds a second signal to the guidance. All-flash array revenue was USD 1.31 billion in the first quarter, up 47.00 percent year over year, while Public Cloud revenue was USD 206.00 million, up 28.00 percent. NetApp's NASDAQ-listed shares had a USD 93.69-216.81 52-week range as of September 30, 2026, with a market capitalization of USD 41.2 billion. The range shows why the new USD 220.00 target is a valuation statement near the upper end of the recent trading band, not a replacement for operating execution. The company also declared a USD 0.52 per-share dividend payable on October 28, 2026, to shareholders of record on October 9, 2026, according to NetApp. For investors, the key tension is visible in the numbers: revenue and AI-linked storage demand are accelerating, while the target increase assumes that higher growth can support a richer earnings multiple.
